cim: U.S. bishops hear update on Church’s efforts to address AI
cim_eredeti: U.S. bishops hear update on Church’s efforts to address AI
szoveg_eredeti:
Bishop Oscar Cantú discussed the work of the USCCB’s AI task force, including its conversations with technology companies and plans for Catholic education and public policy.

BALTIMORE — The U.S. bishops’ task force on artificial intelligence plans to offer formation opportunities for bishops, work with Catholic universities on AI education, and advocate for public policy safeguards, Bishop Oscar Cantú of San José, California, said Nov. 18.

Cantú, chairman of the Task Force on Preserving Human Dignity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, provided an update on the group’s work during the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ (USCCB) fall plenary assembly Nov. 16–19 in Baltimore.

The bishops established the task force in September after meeting with artificial intelligence (AI) experts and representatives of technology companies.

During his presentation, Cantú pointed to Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas as a guide for the task force’s work, particularly as it considers how AI continues to affect human dignity.

“This is a moment that a year ago artificial intelligence was only occasionally in the headlines and today is in multiple headlines every single day,” he told the bishops. “It is dizzying. How do we separate fact from hyperbole? What posture should we take in all of this?”

Cantú said the Church should approach AI with “neither naïve enthusiasm nor unfounded fear” but take part in conversations with technology leaders, public officials, and communities about its effects on society. Pope Leo made a similar appeal in his encyclical, calling on the Church to defend human dignity as the technology advances.

“In the era of artificial intelligence, when human dignity is threatened by new forms of dehumanization, ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human,” the pope wrote. “We must lovingly safeguard the grandeur of humanity bestowed upon us and revealed in its fullness in Christ, the splendor of which no machine can ever replace” (No. 15).

Cantú likened the changes brought by AI to those of the industrial revolution, recalling how the Church responded to that period through Pope Leo XIIIʼs 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum. Rather than oppose industrialization, the Church spoke up for workers’ rights, Cantú pointed out.

“And just as Rerum Novarum ultimately led to concrete results, including minimum wage laws, Social Security, and child labor restrictions,” he said, “Magnifica Humanitas asks us to work for policies and practices that keep artificial intelligence at the service of the human person.”

He said the task force’s meetings with technology companies have gone well so far, with many expressing interest in further conversations about the ethical questions surrounding AI.

One technology leader had a message for the bishops: “Trust your pastoral instincts! Society does not need you to be experts in technology; it needs you to be pastors, who care about your people.”

Cantú said that also means listening to people who are already feeling the effects of AI, including workers, parents, and teachers, rather than leaving the discussion to technology companies.

Among the issues Cantú discussed were the impact of AI on jobs and its potential effects on children, as well as misinformation and autonomous weapons.

He said it is too early to know how much AI will change the workforce but stressed that workers’ rights must remain a concern. Work, he noted, is not just a way to earn a living but also a place where people form relationships and discover their vocations.

He also raised concerns about how growing up with AI could affect children and young people.

“For many young people, artificial intelligence will become a permanent companion,” he said. “Educators and parents are deeply concerned that young people remain capable of critical thought, and that they not lose the capacity for friendship, prayer, and genuine human encounter.”

Cantú also encouraged Catholic educators to develop guidelines for the use of AI in schools. AI-generated images and false information, he warned, could make it increasingly difficult for people to discern what is true.

“The Church, which proclaims Jesus Christ as the truth, must become a school of discernment in the digital age,” he said, adding that “our institutions can be places where people learn to verify, to slow down, and to reason together.”

On autonomous weapons, Cantú cited Pope Leo’s warning that lethal or irreversible decisions should not be entrusted to artificial systems.

The task force plans to offer webinars for bishops and diocesan leaders after the new year, with dates to be announced in the coming weeks. It also hopes to work with Catholic universities to provide formation opportunities and collect best practices for AI education in Catholic schools, seminaries, and universities.

On public policy, the task force will work with the USCCB’s Government Relations team to advocate for safeguards that include transparency, accountability, and human oversight.

The task force is chaired by Cantú and includes Cardinal Blase Cupich of Chicago; Archbishop Paul Etienne of Seattle; Archbishop Shelton Fabre of Louisville, Kentucky; Bishop Barry Knestout of Richmond, Virginia; Auxiliary Bishop James Massa of Brooklyn, New York; Bishop Michael Olson of Fort Worth, Texas; and Auxiliary Bishop Slawomir Szkredka of Los Angeles.

Three academic consultants also advise the group: Charles Camosy of The Catholic University of America; Kim Daniels of Georgetown University’s Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life; and Meghan Sullivan of the University of Notre Dame.

During a Nov. 17 press conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley of Oklahoma City, the USCCB president, also emphasized the importance of maintaining human responsibility in the development and use of AI.

“We are the deciders, if you will,” he said. “We cannot abdicate responsibility to artificial intelligence.”

Archbishop Paul Coakley of Oklahoma City, right, the USCCB president, addresses media during a Nov. 17 press conference at the USCCB fall plenary assembly in Baltimore. Bishop Daniel Flores of Brownsville, Texas, is on the left. | Credit: Jack Haskins/EWTN News

“That’s perhaps the most important thing, to be the human agents that guide and direct artificial intelligence, because artificial intelligence is, in a certain sense, a limitation,” he continued. “The question of human intelligence, which is created by God and God’s image and likeness — it’s ours to guide and direct.”

Cantú urged his fellow bishops to help society keep the human person at the center of discussions about AI.

“Brothers, at a moment when society is asking what machines can do, we must remind the world who the human person is,” he said. “Magnifica Humanitas calls us not to fear the future but to help shape it, with humanity at the center.”
